title: Is Ruby Tuason free of criminal liability?
primary_topics: Ruby Tuason criminal-liability three-tier-analysis column February 16, 2014 -- first of two-part Tuason arc (A425 Feb 16 → A424 Feb 23)

Tuason status: charged with plunder in OOO by DOJ; executed affidavit detailing participation + implicating coconspirators + offering to return P40M share of loot (admitted to Senate blue ribbon committee)

Three-tier role-analysis structure: (1) DOJ's role (WPP grant with cross-examination condition) (2) Ombudsman's role (sole indictment discretion + RA 6770 immunity) (3) Sandiganbayan's role (discharge-as-state's-witness 5-requisite test)

DOJ + WPP: De Lima granted WPP benefits on condition Tuason would testify and be cross-examined in court; WPP Law (RA 6981) benefits enumerated -- free housing + 24-hour security + financial assistance + traveling expenses + medical treatment + 'relocation and/or change of identity at expense of Program'
WPP 'not most guilty' test + admission entitles witness 'to immunity from criminal prosecution' provided compliance with MOA undertakings

Ombudsman's role: DOJ can no longer exclude Tuason from complaint because OOO has assumed jurisdiction; in cases involving public officials and coconspirators (may be private people), OOO 'as a rule conducts preliminary investigation' + has discretion to determine probable cause + select who should/should not be charged; OOO has prerogative to determine whether to include Tuason in information
Separate law RA 6770 authorizes OOO to grant immunity to coperpetrators; 'in short, Tuason's immunity from prosecution depends on the OOO, no longer on the DOJ'

Sandiganbayan's role: if OOO includes Tuason in information, SBN per Rules of Court may still discharge her as accused 'provided the court is convinced' -- 5 requisites: (a) absolute necessity for testimony (b) no other available direct evidence (c) testimony substantially corroborable (d) not most guilty (e) no moral-turpitude conviction

Plunder capital + 'nonbailable'; SBN can require OOO to present evidence to 'convince' court that 5 requisites complied with; once discharged becomes state's witness + released from detention; 'a discharge made by the court shall amount to an acquittal of the discharged accused and shall be a bar to future litigation for the same offense' -- courts grant acquittal vs DOJ/OOO grant only 'immunity from prosecution'

'More on DAP' coda: enterprising readers googled CJP's Separate Opinion in Sanlakas v. Exec. Sec. (Feb 3, 2004) about 'capable of repetition yet evading review' exception; Lacson v. Perez (May 10, 2001) hybrid disposition precedent (dismissed mooted cases but 'enjoined government from arresting petitioners... without required judicial warrants'); CJP's 'writings are not intended to spoon-feed readers' pedagogical-philosophy close
sub_topics: Ruby Tuason, who has been charged with plunder in OOO by DOJ, executed affidavit detailing her participation in crime
Implicating some of her alleged coconspirators and offering to return her share of loot
Which she admitted to Senate blue ribbon committee as about P40 million
Is she now free of criminal liability?
Short answer: No, not yet
But to begin with, Justice Sec. Leila de Lima granted her benefits of government's Witness Protection Program (WPP)
On condition that she would testify and be cross-examined in court to validate her affidavit
DOJ, with backing of Malacañang, believes Tuason's affidavit and putative testimony would corroborate, affirm and strengthen charge against principal offenders
And would result in their conviction in what is expected to be long and tedious litigation
WPP Law (RA 6981) authorizes DOJ to extend several benefits to potential witnesses and their immediate family
Including free housing, 24-hour security, financial assistance, traveling expenses, medical treatment
And if needed, 'relocation and/or change of identity at expense of Program'
Witnesses who participated in crime (like Tuason) must 'not appear to be the most guilty'
Admission into program entitles witnesses 'to immunity from criminal prosecution'
Provided they comply with their undertakings in 'memorandum of agreement' they executed with DOJ
To repeat, Tuason has been included as respondent in plunder complaint filed in OOO by DOJ
Thus, DOJ can no longer exclude her from complaint because OOO has assumed jurisdiction over case
In cases involving public officials and their coconspirators (who may be private people)
OOO, as a rule, conducts preliminary investigation
It therefore has discretion to determine existence of probable cause
And to select who should or should not be charged in Sandiganbayan
Consequently, it is OOO that has prerogative to determine whether to include her in any information
Separate law (RA 6770) authorizes OOO to grant immunity to coperpetrators
In short, Tuason's immunity from prosecution depends on OOO, no longer on DOJ
If OOO decides to include Tuason in information
SBN -- per Rules of Court -- may still discharge her as accused
'Provided the court is convinced' that:
(a) there is absolute necessity for her testimony
(b) there is no other available direct evidence
(c) her testimony can be substantially corroborated
(d) she does not appear to be most guilty
(e) she has not been convicted of any offense involving moral turpitude
Once information that includes her is filed, Tuason like all other accused, may be arrested and detained
Possibly in WPP safe house, because plunder is capital and 'nonbailable' offense
Moreover, SBN can require OOO to present evidence to 'convince' court that five requisites had been complied with
However, once discharged by court to become state's witness, she would be released from detention
Discharge made by court shall amount to acquittal of discharged accused
And shall be bar to future litigation for same offense
In short, courts grant acquittal to discharged accused
While DOJ and OOO give merely 'immunity from prosecution'
More on DAP: CJP wrote last Sunday that, as retired jurist, he would not venture opinion on whether DAP cases should now be dismissed for having become 'moot and academic'
Because SC has not finished hearing parties; another oral argument set on Feb 18
But enterprising readers googled CJP's Separate Opinion in Sanlakas v. Exec. Sec. (Feb 3, 2004)
Which said mooted case 'capable of repetition yet evading review' may still be decided by Court
'Provided the party raising it has been, or continues to be, prejudiced or damaged'
Consequently, venturing opinion now is premature since parties have not completed their arguments
CJP needs to see whether petitioners have been personally prejudiced or injured by government's mooted actions
Others perceptively opined petitioners have not shown any direct personal injury
Ergo, DAP cases should now be dismissed for having become moot and academic
For future guidance of officials, CJP thinks Court, while dismissing mooted petitions, may still tackle two important issues:
(1) nature of savings that can be realigned, and
(2) validity of cross-border transfer of funds
Court made this hybrid disposition in Lacson v. Perez (May 10, 2001) when it dismissed mooted cases
But 'enjoined [government] from arresting petitioners... without required judicial warrants'
Both Sanlakas and Lacson cases were taken up in CJP's said column
Many now know that CJP's writings are not intended to spoon-feed readers
CJP expects them to reach their conclusions on basis of discussions he presents
Does not wish to mesmerize them into adopting his opinions
Rather, prefers them to analyze, think and make their own conclusions
CJP humbly believes this is better way of opining and teaching

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the first installment of his two-part Ruby-Tuason arc (followed by A424 Feb 23), structured as a three-tier role-analysis: DOJ + OOO + SBN. Ruby Tuason, who has been charged with plunder in the OOO by the DOJ, executed an affidavit detailing her participation in the crime, implicating some of her alleged coconspirators, and offering to return her share of the loot, which she admitted to the Senate blue ribbon committee as about P40 million -- is she now free of criminal liability? CJ's short answer: No, not yet. DOJ's role: Justice Sec. Leila de Lima granted her the benefits of the government's WPP on the condition that she would testify and be cross-examined in court to validate her affidavit; the DOJ, with the backing of Malacañang, believes Tuason's affidavit and putative testimony would corroborate, affirm and strengthen the charge against the principal offenders and would result in their conviction in what is expected to be a long and tedious litigation. The WPP Law (RA 6981) authorizes the DOJ to extend several benefits to potential witnesses and their immediate family, including free housing, 24-hour security, financial assistance, traveling expenses, medical treatment, and if needed, 'relocation and/or change of identity at the expense of the Program.' Witnesses who participated in the crime (like Tuason) must 'not appear to be the most guilty'; admission into the program entitles the witnesses 'to immunity from criminal prosecution' provided they comply with their undertakings in the MOA they executed with the DOJ. Ombudsman's role: to repeat, Tuason has been included as a respondent in the plunder complaint filed in the OOO by the DOJ -- thus, the DOJ can no longer exclude her from the complaint because the OOO has assumed jurisdiction over the case; in cases involving public officials and their coconspirators (who may be private people), the OOO 'as a rule conducts the preliminary investigation'; it therefore has the discretion to determine the existence of probable cause and to select who should or should not be charged in the SBN; consequently, it is the OOO that has the prerogative to determine whether to include her in any information; a separate law (RA 6770) authorizes the OOO to grant immunity to coperpetrators -- in short, Tuason's immunity from prosecution depends on the OOO, no longer on the DOJ. Sandiganbayan's role: if the OOO decides to include Tuason in the information, the SBN -- per the Rules of Court -- may still discharge her as an accused, 'provided the court is convinced' that (a) there is absolute necessity for her testimony; (b) there is no other available direct evidence; (c) her testimony can be substantially corroborated; (d) she does not appear to be the most guilty; and (e) she has not been convicted of any offense involving moral turpitude. Once the information that includes her is filed, Tuason, like all the other accused, may be arrested and detained, possibly in the WPP safe house, because plunder is a capital and 'nonbailable' offense; moreover, the SBN can require the OOO to present evidence to 'convince' the court that the five requisites had been complied with; however, once discharged by the court to become a state's witness, she would be released from detention. A discharge made by the court shall amount to an acquittal of the discharged accused and shall be a bar to future litigation for the same offense -- in short, courts grant acquittal to the discharged accused while the DOJ and the OOO give merely 'immunity from prosecution.' More on DAP: CJ wrote last Sunday (A426) that, as a retired jurist, he would not venture an opinion on whether the DAP cases should now be dismissed for having become 'moot and academic' because the SC has not finished hearing the parties -- another oral argument is set on Feb 18. But enterprising readers googled CJ's Separate Opinion in Sanlakas v. Exec. Sec. (Feb 3, 2004) which said that a mooted case 'capable of repetition yet evading review' may still be decided by the Court 'provided the party raising it has been, or continues to be, prejudiced or damaged' -- consequently, venturing an opinion now is premature since the parties have not completed their arguments; CJ needs to see whether the petitioners have been personally prejudiced or injured by the government's mooted actions. Others perceptively opined that the petitioners have not shown any direct personal injury, ergo the DAP cases should now be dismissed for having become moot and academic. For the future guidance of our officials, CJ thinks the Court, while dismissing the mooted petitions, may still tackle two important issues: (1) the nature of the savings that can be realigned, and (2) the validity of cross-border transfer of funds. The Court made this hybrid disposition in Lacson v. Perez (May 10, 2001) when it dismissed the mooted cases but 'enjoined [the government] from arresting the petitioners... without the required judicial warrants...'; both the Sanlakas and the Lacson cases were taken up in CJ's said column. Many now know that CJ's writings are not intended to spoon-feed readers -- CJ expects them to reach their conclusions on the basis of the discussions he presents; he does not wish to mesmerize them into adopting his opinions; rather, he prefers them to analyze, think and make their own conclusions; CJ humbly believes this is the better way of opining and teaching.
